title: No-TSV shingled staircase stack with printed edge ramps
idea: Eliminate TSVs: offset each DRAM die ~200 um like roof shingles so every die exposes a ledge of fine-pitch pads, then plate or aerosol-jet-print copper 'ramps' down the stairs to the base die at 10-20 um pitch, using several ledge rows for a 1024-bit bus. No via etch, no via reveal, no keep-out zones.
why: HBM TSV tax (3x wafer area/bit, 20-30% yield loss): recovers the ~10-15% of die area spent on TSV arrays and keep-out, removes via-reveal steps and their yield loss; claimed ~20-30% lower HBM cost/bit.

title: Bookshelf memory: dies stand on edge atop compute
idea: Eliminate both the interposer and TSVs: route top-metal lines to a polished, metallized die edge carrying ~2 um-pitch pads, stand dozens of DRAM dies vertically on the GPU's top surface and hybrid-bond their edges; the gaps between the standing dies become microfluidic coolant channels, so the memory doubles as a heat-sink fin array.
why: A 10 mm x 100 um edge offers ~250k contacts per die (more than a whole HBM stack) with zero TSV area and no interposer; vertical wire length <100 um targets <0.3 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM and attacks the TSV tax.

title: Array-only DRAM sensed directly by the processor's sense amplifiers
idea: Eliminate the memory die's periphery and PHY: the DRAM die carries only cells, local bitlines and wordline stubs; every 32-bitline group feeds a local charge-transfer pre-amp to one ~1 um hybrid-bond pad, and the sense amps, decoders and row buffers live in the logic die beneath on fast low-voltage transistors. The 'interface' is a bitline.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die and IO is 3-4 pJ/bit: removing both gives ~1.8-2x bits per DRAM wafer, puts the row buffer next to compute and drops movement to ~0.1 pJ/bit.

title: Clockless delay-insensitive memory channel without DLLs or training
idea: Eliminate the clock: replace DDR strobes, DLLs, PLLs and link training on short on-package links with a 1-of-4 delay-insensitive code (2 bits on 4 wires, one transition per symbol, receiver detects completion and acknowledges). Timing adapts automatically to voltage, temperature and process.
why: Clocking and training are ~20-30% of PHY power/area and idle clocks burn energy; a self-timed link targets ~0.3 pJ/bit with zero idle power and permits aggressive voltage scaling below today's IO floor.

title: Address-free streaming: tensor descriptors replace per-access addresses
idea: Eliminate per-access command/address traffic: the host writes one descriptor (base, strides, tile shape, dtype) into the HBM base die, which generates its own ACT/RD sequences and streams data in consumption order, exploiting bank-interleave knowledge only the memory has.
why: Command/address pins and reorder queues are dead weight for AI streams: removes ~15-20% of channel pins and controller queue area; memory-side scheduling avoids row conflicts for ~20-30% more effective bandwidth.

title: Infrared through-silicon optical vias replace TSV stacks
idea: Eliminate copper vias: silicon is transparent at 1.3 um, so each thinned die carries Ge photodiodes and micro-emitters in metal-free windows; beams pass straight through intervening dies to receivers on the target die, addressed by position or wavelength.
why: Removes TSV area, via reveal, stress keep-out zones and TSV-driven stack yield loss (HBM TSV tax); no capacitive load on vertical links, claimed <0.5 pJ/bit vertical.

title: Solderless nano-velcro interconnect makes HBM socketable and reworkable
idea: Eliminate solder and permanent bonding: grow interlocking copper nanohook forests on memory and logic pads (~5 um pitch) that mesh mechanically at room temperature under clamp pressure and can be unclipped; a failed or outgrown stack is swapped instead of scrapping a $30k GPU package.
why: HBM package yield loss (20-30%) compounds over 8 stacks; reworkability recovers most of it and lets memory be sold/upgraded separately from compute, claimed ~15-25% lower effective cost/bit.

title: Driverless memory die read by host-powered backscatter
idea: Eliminate the DRAM's output drivers: the processor launches a carrier on each DQ line and the memory die only toggles a tiny switch that changes the line's termination impedance (like an RFID tag), so the reflected wave carries the data; all transmit energy and big driver transistors sit on the logic die.
why: DRAM-process transistors make slow, power-hungry drivers; shifting transmit to better logic transistors at lower voltage cuts read IO energy ~30-50% and frees driver area on the DRAM die.

title: Series voltage-stacked DRAM dies eliminate most power TSVs
idea: Eliminate low-voltage high-current power delivery: stack 12 dies electrically in series across a ~13 V rail so each die floats in its own ~1.1 V domain and the same current is recycled through all dies; on-die switched-capacitor balancers absorb mismatch and capacitive level shifters carry data between domains.
why: Power/ground TSVs are a large share of HBM TSVs and IR drop caps stack height; 12x lower current cuts power TSV count up to ~10x, shrinking TSV area tax and enabling taller stacks.

title: Bit-plane progressive fetch stops when precision suffices
idea: Eliminate low-order bits from the bus: store tensors transposed into bit-planes and fetch sign/exponent/MSB planes first; the consumer's datapath signals 'enough' as soon as the result (e.g., top-k ordering or a dot-product bound) can no longer change, and the remaining planes are never sent.
why: Data movement is 20-25% of accelerator power: on LLM decode ~40-60% of mantissa bits are provably unnecessary per operation, cutting bytes moved ~1.5-2x without fixed quantization loss.

title: Memory-side top-k gate returns token indices, not keys
idea: Eliminate shipping full key vectors: each HBM pseudo-channel's base-die slice holds a small dot-product unit and comparator tree that scores the query against stored keys inside the stack and returns only the top-k token indices; only those value rows then cross the interface.
why: Long-context KV reads dominate decode bandwidth; for k=64 of 128k tokens interface traffic falls >10x for ~3-5% base-die area.

title: ESD-free hybrid-bond IO for wafer-level-only stacks
idea: Eliminate ESD protection on internal die-to-die pads: hybrid-bonded faces are never touched by humans or probes after bonding, so drop ESD diodes and use a sacrificial wafer-level discharge grid that is severed during bonding, shrinking pad capacitance from ~200 fF to ~10 fF.
why: IO energy is CV^2 dominated by pad capacitance: vertical-link energy/bit falls ~5-10x and smaller pads allow 2-3x more vertical channels in the same area.

title: Thirteenth-die hot spare rescues HBM stack yield
idea: Eliminate 'one bad die scraps the stack': build 12-high stacks with a 13th identical spare die and a vertical channel crossbar in the base die; after final stack test, a failing die's channels are steered onto the spare.
why: HBM yield is down 20-30%: with 97% per-die post-bond survival, stack yield rises from ~69% (0.97^12) to ~94% with one spare, cutting effective cost/bit ~25%.

title: Simultaneous bidirectional DQ: reads and writes share each wire
idea: Eliminate bus turnaround and half the data pins: both ends drive each on-package lane at once and subtract their own known transmitted signal with a hybrid echo canceller (as gigabit Ethernet does), so reads and writes flow concurrently on the same wire.
why: Removes tWTR/tRTW bubbles (~10-15% bandwidth loss on mixed traffic) and allows halving DQ count or doubling bandwidth per mm of beachfront.

title: Air-gap interposer wiring cuts per-bit wire capacitance
idea: Eliminate the dielectric between HBM-to-GPU interposer lines: after patterning, selectively etch a sacrificial polymer to leave lines suspended in air (k~1 vs ~3.5) on periodic support posts, then seal with a cap layer.
why: On-interposer link energy is dominated by wire capacitance: ~3x lower C gives ~2-3x lower pJ/bit and permits longer reach, so more stacks can surround one GPU.

title: Orthogonal-access memory reads rows or columns, killing transposes
idea: Eliminate transpose and relayout copies: each cell in a dedicated tile gets two access devices on orthogonal wordline/bitline pairs (dual-port 2T gain cell), so a weight tile is read row-major in the forward pass and column-major in the backward pass without being moved.
why: Transposes and layout shuffles cost an extra read+write of tensors (~10-20% of training traffic); a small dual-port region at ~1.5x cell area removes that traffic.

title: Charge-coupled shift memory streams KV cache without decoders
idea: Eliminate row/column decoders and the address bus for sequential data: store KV-cache pages in CCD-style buried-channel charge-transfer registers that shift packets to one sense node per lane each clock, reviving 1970s CCD memory on modern CMOS-image-sensor lines.
why: Decode reads are sequential scans: CCD cells need no access transistor and no decoder (periphery ~49%), circulation implies refresh, and 40-65 nm CIS fabs need no EUV and exist in the U.S.

title: Controller-less DRAM: compiler emits cycle-exact raw memory commands
idea: Eliminate the memory controller's queues, reorder logic and refresh scheduler: for static AI graphs the compiler schedules every ACT/RD/WR/REF at cycle level with temperature-guarded margins, and the PHY simply replays the command stream.
why: Controllers cost SoC area/power and add 20-40 ns latency plus variance; deterministic schedules reach >90% bus utilization and return the area to compute or SRAM.

title: NIC inside the HBM base die for direct remote writes
idea: Eliminate the GPU hop for network data: put a co-packaged optical RDMA engine in each HBM base die so remote nodes write KV caches, gradients and activations directly into the target stack without crossing the GPU's PHY and NoC twice.
why: Removes ~2 extra interface crossings per byte (~6-8 pJ/bit saved) and frees GPU beachfront from network SerDes for more memory.

title: Micro-HBM carpet: dozens of tiny stacks over the die
idea: Eliminate the beachfront limit and interposer distance: instead of 8 large edge stacks, hybrid-bond ~64 small 4-high 1-2 GB stacks directly over the compute die's area with thermal pillars between them, each feeding the tile beneath it.
why: Wire length drops from ~5 mm to ~50 um and IO energy from 3-4 to ~0.2 pJ/bit; 4-high stacks yield far better than 12-high and need no interposer.

title: Dual-ported HBM shared by neighboring GPUs ends stranded capacity
idea: Eliminate fixed one-GPU ownership of HBM: a base die with two PHYs links a stack to two adjacent GPU packages via a bridge, so capacity flows to whichever GPU needs it (KV cache on one, weights on the other).
why: Fleet HBM utilization is often 50-70%; pairwise pooling recovers ~15-25% capacity, so fewer DRAM bits are bought per useful bit.

title: Wireless mm-wave weight broadcast to many chiplets at once
idea: Eliminate per-consumer copies and point-to-point wires for read-shared data: one memory chiplet broadcasts weight tiles over a 200-300 GHz on-package antenna and waveguide cavity, and 16-64 compute chiplets receive the same bits simultaneously.
why: Parallel inference fetches the same weights N times and replicates them in N local memories; broadcast cuts weight traffic and replicated capacity by ~N.

title: Second-life DRAM: retired server DIMMs reborn as CXL pools
idea: Eliminate new wafers for the capacity tier: strip DDR4/DDR5 chips from decommissioned servers, screen with burn-in and row-hammer tests, and mount them behind CXL Type-3 controllers that translate protocol and map out weak rows.
why: Huge volumes of DRAM are retired yearly; reusing it as a slower tier raises usable supply with zero fab capex and spares new DDR5/HBM for hot data, at ~5-10x lower cost/bit than today's 4x contract price.

title: Via-ROM weight chiplet: frozen weights need no DRAM
idea: Eliminate DRAM, its writes and its refresh for deployed model weights: encode weights in a single custom via-mask layer of a mature-node ROM die (one via = one bit) hybrid-bonded under the compute die; the data survives power loss by construction.
why: Weights are ~60-80% of inference memory; via-ROM is ~5x cheaper per bit than DRAM, needs one 28-40 nm mask (no EUV, U.S.-fabbable) and reads at ~0.1 pJ/bit over hybrid bonds.

title: Refresh-piggybacked mirroring into a bonded non-volatile twin layer
idea: Eliminate the separate backup flush: a ferroelectric or MRAM twin layer bonded under each bank receives a row copy whenever that row is refreshed and its dirty bit is set (the row is already open, so only the vertical transfer is paid); at power loss only rows dirtied since their last refresh are flushed, within the PSU's existing ~10 ms hold-up energy.
why: Gives DRAM speed and endurance with full non-volatility, removing NVDIMM batteries/supercaps and 30-s serial flushes; copying rides on refresh activations, so no extra ACT energy or row-hammer exposure.

title: Non-volatile write FIFO in the PHY makes pins persistent
idea: Eliminate cache-flush and fence round trips: put a small ferroelectric-capacitor-backed write queue in the controller PHY and memory base die so a write is durable the moment it crosses the pins; the queue drains to the NV array at leisure and replays after power loss.
why: Persistent-memory software pays ~0.1-1 us per CLWB+SFENCE and doubles traffic with write-ahead logs; durable in-flight path cuts commit latency ~5-10x and removes log write amplification.

title: Magnetic stray-field vias couple stacked MRAM dies
idea: Eliminate TSVs in a non-volatile stack: each die carries 'transmitter' nanomagnet columns switched by spin-orbit torque, and the die above senses their stray field with TMR sensors across a thinned-die/bond gap of a few um; the vertical link itself holds state with zero power.
why: Removes TSV area tax and via reveal; vertical signalling at ~fJ switching energy. Field decays steeply over microns, so this is a long shot.

title: Interposer that remembers: BEOL non-volatile memory inside it
idea: Eliminate the interposer's passivity: the ~2500 mm2 silicon interposer (65 nm-class, cheap, U.S.-fabbable) becomes an active interposer with BEOL MRAM or HZO FeRAM arrays and simple peripheral CMOS under and between chiplets, stacking 3-4 BEOL array layers.
why: Adds ~5-8 GB of NV capacity 1-2 mm from compute without extra dies, packages or EUV, reusing area that is today pure wiring, at ~0.5 pJ/bit.

title: Checkpoint-in-place: non-volatile HBM ends training checkpoint traffic
idea: Eliminate copying model and optimizer state to storage: on NV-cell HBM, a checkpoint is a metadata flip that seals a copy-on-write page epoch inside the stack, so no checkpoint bytes leave the package; recovery remaps to the last sealed epoch.
why: Big training runs spend ~5-15% of time and huge network/storage bandwidth writing TB-scale checkpoints every ~30 min; removing them raises cluster goodput and deletes the checkpoint storage tier.

title: Retention-dial memory: one die is both DRAM and storage
idea: Eliminate the DRAM-to-SSD copy and the two-chip BOM: use a spin-torque or ferroelectric cell whose write pulse width/amplitude sets retention (short pulse: hours, ~1e15 endurance, ns writes; long pulse: 10 years), with the base die re-writing pages in long-retention mode as they cool.
why: Removes storage-to-memory transfers and duplicate copies across tiers; in phones and edge devices one package replaces LPDDR+UFS, saving ~30% memory BOM and all load-time traffic.

title: Latching phase-change optical switches pool memory at zero hold power
idea: Eliminate the always-on electrical switch in memory pooling: build the rack's memory fabric from GST-clad silicon-photonic switches whose routing state latches non-volatilely, so host-to-memory assignments persist through power loss and cost no energy to hold.
why: Pooling recovers ~20-30% stranded DRAM; latching optics remove switch-ASIC power and post-outage re-discovery, making pooled memory cheaper to run than local.

title: Analog pass-through: multilevel NV cells drive PAM4 lanes directly
idea: Eliminate digitization and re-encoding between cell and wire: a 2-bit/cell FeFET array is sensed into four voltage levels that are buffered straight onto a PAM4 lane through an analog mux, and the receiver's slicer performs the only quantization.
why: Removes sense-to-digital-to-serializer stages (~30-40% of read-path energy) and doubles bits per symbol per cell access, while data stays non-volatile.

title: Bond-level non-volatile repair switches heal failed hybrid bonds
idea: Eliminate scrapping stacks for a few bad vertical connections: place tiny ReRAM/antifuse crosspoint switches beside every 16 hybrid-bond pads plus 2 spares, programmed after post-bond test to route around opens and shorts; routing persists without power or e-fuse reload.
why: At 1-3 um pitch with millions of bonds, bond defects dominate stack yield; per-group sparing pushes vertical-link yield >99.9%, attacking the 20-30% HBM yield loss.

title: Non-volatile PHY state enables nanosecond link sleep and wake
idea: Eliminate link retraining: store each lane's DFE taps, CTLE settings, phase offsets and VREF in ferroelectric latches inside the PHY, so the entire memory PHY can be power-gated between bursts and resume in <100 ns with no retraining.
why: PHYs burn ~20-30% of interface power idling to stay trained; gating between bursts cuts average IO energy ~30% on bursty inference traffic.

title: Memory cartridges: ship non-volatile modules instead of moving bytes
idea: Eliminate the network for bulk model distribution: package NV HBM-class stacks on hot-pluggable carriers written once at a central site and physically installed into inference servers, which execute directly from them as working memory.
why: A courier of 1 TB cartridges beats replicating a model to 10k servers over the network; removes petabytes of rollout traffic and boot-time weight loading.

title: Ferroelectric content-addressable KV store returns matches, not data
idea: Eliminate scanning KV caches over the bus: store quantized key signatures in 2-FeFET ternary CAM cells so a query is broadcast into the array and only matching token addresses come out; the index survives power cycles.
why: For sparse retrieval and long-context attention, interface traffic falls ~100x and persistent RAG indexes need no reload after power events.

title: ADC-free time-domain readout of ferroelectric weight crossbars
idea: Eliminate the ADCs that dominate compute-in-memory: stationary NV weights in a FeFET crossbar discharge a precharged column at a rate proportional to the dot product, and a pulse-width output feeds the next layer or a time-to-digital counter.
why: Weights never move; ADCs are 50-80% of CIM energy/area, so removing them makes in-memory MACs ~5x more efficient than shipping weights at 3-4 pJ/bit.

title: All-optical writes to magnetic memory through on-chip waveguides
idea: Eliminate electrical write drivers: deliver femtosecond laser pulses via silicon-nitride waveguides to GdFeCo-based MTJ free layers that toggle by all-optical switching; reads stay electrical via TMR.
why: Write data arriving on a photonic link is stored without O/E conversion, pushing write energy toward tens of fJ/bit and removing write-driver area.

title: Spin-wave buses carry data between MRAM banks without charge
idea: Eliminate charge-carrying wires between NV banks: CoFeB or YIG magnonic waveguides move data as spin-wave phase from one bank's MTJ transducers to others, with interference-based fan-out to many banks at once.
why: Inter-bank copies and broadcasts at ~aJ-fJ per bit with no Joule heating in wires.

title: One shared non-volatile weight copy mapped by sixteen hosts
idea: Eliminate per-server weight copies: a CXL 3.x multi-headed NV memory device holds a model once and 16 hosts map it read-only; hosts keep only KV caches and activations in local DRAM.
why: Inference fleets replicate 100s of GB of identical weights on every node; one copy per 16 hosts cuts weight DRAM up to ~16x, and NV means no reload after maintenance or outages.

title: Epoch-tagged dual-slot lines make crash consistency fence-free
idea: Eliminate persist barriers and write-ahead logging: each NV line has two slots; writes go to the uncommitted slot tagged with a hardware epoch, and a single per-epoch commit record flips which slot is valid, so recovery discards incomplete epochs automatically.
why: Logging doubles NV write traffic and fences stall pipelines; dual-slot epochs halve write bandwidth for persistent data structures and remove ordering stalls (~2x throughput).

title: Die passport: on-die non-volatile test history ends retesting
idea: Eliminate repeated testing at every packaging step: each memory die carries a small OTP/ReRAM log written at wafer sort, burn-in and post-bond test (bin, repair map, timing margins, weak rows), read by the stacker and later by the system.
why: Test is ~10-20% of memory cost and HBM retests dies several times; passports cut test time ~30-50%, and systems use the weak-row map to avoid extra refresh.

title: Grid-flexible datacenters: non-volatile memory lets racks drop at peaks
idea: Eliminate the 'stay powered to keep state' requirement: with NV working memory, racks cut to zero power within milliseconds on utility demand-response signals and resume exactly where they were; policy lets utilities fast-track interconnection for certified interruptible NV-equipped load.
why: Grid power is now the binding constraint on new AI capacity; interruptible load connects years sooner and needs far less UPS battery, freeing capital and energy.

title: Append-only KV log on NAND bonded beneath HBM
idea: Eliminate the flash translation layer and the SSD path for KV-cache spill: bond 3D NAND under the HBM base die and write KV caches as append-only logs aligned to erase blocks, erasing whole blocks when conversations expire, which matches NAND's native semantics so no mapping table, GC or write amplification is needed.
why: KV spill to SSD crosses PCIe at ~10-30 pJ/bit; in-stack NAND gives ~10x capacity per package at NAND cost/bit with only one fresh write per token.

title: Photonic phase-change memory read by light without conversion
idea: Eliminate O/E/O conversion at disaggregated memory: store bits in GST or Sb2Se3 patches on silicon-nitride waveguides whose phase state sets transmission, and read them with WDM light pulses arriving directly from compute.
why: Read is just attenuation with no modulator or photodiode at the memory, cutting link-plus-access energy toward ~1 pJ/bit; ~1e8-1e12 endurance limits it to read-mostly data.

title: Switch-side erasure coding replaces triple-replicated persistent memory
idea: Eliminate 3x replication traffic for durable in-memory state: the CXL switch stripes NV memory writes across 10+4 Reed-Solomon shards on different modules and computes parity in the switch, so state survives power loss and module failure.
why: Durable caches replicate over the network 3x; switch-side erasure coding needs 1.4x instead of 3x capacity and cuts durability bytes moved ~2x.
